The Irish DPA posed an administrative fine of €1500 on Men Overcoming Violence Ireland ("MOVE") for the failure to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures when recording group sessions in violation of Article 5(1)(f) GDPR and Article 32(1) GDPR.

The Spanish DPA fined a controller acting on behalf of Vodafone €20,000 for making unsolicited commercial calls to a data subject. The controller failed to adequately check phone numbers against a list of users who did not wish to receive calls.

The Norwegian DPA instructed Google to delete a search result about a data subject's criminal past, but agreed with their decision to refuse erasure for two other search results. The DPA agreed these were still relevant after 10 years, in part because the data subject was a CSO in a company planning to go public, and the information was deemed to be of public interest. The Privacy Appeals Board later upheld the DPA's decision.

The Austrian DPA held that, according to the circumstances of this case, a controller did not violate Articles 4(11), 6(1)(a) and 7 GDPR by using a pre-ticked box, because the purpose of this box was to give the data subject the opportunity to object against the processing under Article 21 GDPR and not to obtain its consent.
The UK DPA fined a direct marketing company approximately €58,600 (£50,000) for making illegal marketing calls to people about their pensions.

The Norwegian DPA fined a beauty salon approximately €9,473 (NOK 100,000) for unlawfully installing camera surveillance that gave the general manager constant live access to images and sound via a mobile app on her phone, without informing employees or customers. Following an appeal, the Norwegian Privacy Appeals Board upheld the DPA's decision.

The Hungarian DPA held that a data subject was entitled to have their personal data deleted from recordings and transcripts of an open hearing at a Budapest district assembly. In particular, it considered the disclosure of their name and address during those meetings to be in breach of the principle of data minimisation.
The Spanish DPA fined a gymnastics club €5,000 for posting images of two children on its Instagram page, despite the express denial of consent by their mother.
The DPA held that a controller unlawfully processed a data subject’s personal data by failing to inform the data subject of the collection from a job advertisement portal.

The Finnish DPA issued a warning against a housing company that required residents diagnosed with coronavirus to inform the property manager. It considered other measures unnecessary because no such data was actually collected.

A customer complained that an insurer's employee had twice emailed health-related information and medical forms to wrong email addresses. The CNPD opened an investigation, inspected the premises in July 2019 and found failures on email security, breach documentation, breach notification, communication to the data subject and DPO contact details. The restricted formation imposed a fine of EUR 135,000 based on Articles 5(1)(f), 32(1)(a) and (b) and 33(5) GDPR. It did not base the fine on the Article 33(1), 34(1) and 37(7) breaches, though it found them. It also ordered the insurer to secure emails containing special-category data within two months. The investigation head had proposed EUR 275,000.
The Austrian DPA imposed a fine of €600 on an individual for unlawfully disclosing the medical data of a data subject to the latter's employer.

The Romanian DPA fined a natural person approximately €200 (RON 985.5) for disclosing copies of a pay slip and a kindergarten register containing personal data on their personal Facebook page and via flyers they distributed, in in violation of Articles 5, 6 and 14 GDPR.
The Spanish DPA fined the owner of a dating website €2000 for publishing contact data without the consent of the data subject.

The Spanish DPA fined Vodafone €120,000 (reduced to €96,000) for processing personal data without a legal basis, since they did not prevent a third party from fraudulently using someone's personal data to contract its service, and for not complying with the right to erasure.

The Belgian DPA closed a case regarding the use of a municipality database for a political campaign, despite finding a violation of the purpose limitation principle. The case involved two defendants, and it could not be established that the first defendant had used the database for the campaign. The second defendant, who did have access to the database, died after the complaint.

The Spanish DPA fined a controller €60,000 for failing to respond to an access request, and for processing personal data without a legal basis, since it could not prove it had entered into a contract with the data subject.

The French DPA fined Monsanto €400,000 for creating files containing the personal data of more than 200 French and European political figures for the purpose of lobbying, without informing the data subjects, and without executing a data processing agreement with the relevant processor.

The AEPD investigated Mercadona's facial recognition system in its stores, which was meant to detect people with final convictions and restraining orders against the company or its staff. It found that the processing of special-category biometric data was prohibited and lacked a legal basis, that information to data subjects was inadequate, that data minimisation and data protection by design were breached, and that the impact assessment was deficient. A fine of EUR 2,000,000 + 100,000 + 500,000 + 500,000 + 50,000 = EUR 3,150,000 was proposed. Mercadona paid voluntarily with a 20% reduction (EUR 2,520,000), which ended the procedure. The AEPD also prohibited all facial recognition processing in its stores.

After an ex officio investigation and an on-site inspection in June 2019, the Italian DPA examined how Deliveroo Italy processes the personal data of its roughly 8,000 riders through a platform run centrally by the UK parent. It found breaches of the processing principles, transparency, safeguards for automated decision-making and profiling, privacy by design, records of processing, security, impact assessment, DPO notification and the employment-context and remote-monitoring rules. It ordered the company to bring its processing into compliance within set deadlines and imposed a fine of EUR 2,500,000, with publication of the order.
The Italian DPA (Garante) imposed a fine of €200,000 on the Region of Lombardia (Italy) for publishing personal data of students requiring financial contributions on its website.

Following a report, the Garante investigated the new parking meters in Rome, which require drivers to enter the vehicle plate. It found that Roma Capitale, as controller, gave no adequate privacy notice, had not appointed ATAC and Flowbird as processors under Article 28, had set no retention periods (8.6 million parking records were stored), and used weak security (unencrypted http transfers, plaintext short passwords, no access logs, MD5 hashing of old plates). The Garante found violations of Articles 5, 12, 13, 25, 28 and 32 GDPR, fined Roma Capitale EUR 800,000, ordered corrective security measures within 30 days and ordered publication of the decision.

The French DPA fined an insurance and supplementary pension firm €1,750,000 for violating the data retention principle in Article 5. Although it also investigated the firm for violations of Articles 13 and 14 GDPR, it did not fine the firm for these violations since it implemented adequate measures to comply during the course of the procedure.

The Belgian DPA issued a new decision following a so-called 'light decision', whereby it had ordered a company to stop processing certain personal data used for direct marketing and to delete the data. Since the company neither complied with the order nor notified the DPA of any action taken, it issued a new decision, with a reprimand and a new order to comply within one month.

The EDPB adopted an urgent binding decision under Article 66 GDPR. Following a provisional measure taken by the Hamburg DPA against WhatsApp, the EDPB analysed WhatsApp's data sharing practices with Facebook. The EDPB did not confirm the provisional measure, but given the high likelihood that data sharing is taking place, it requested the Irish DPA to investigate certain key blind spots in WhatsApp's data processing, including whether data is actually shared with Facebook, whether Facebook acts as processor or joint controller, and whether the legal basis identified in the privacy policy is adequate in relation to the actual processing.

The Danish DPA fined Medicals Nordic approximately €80,500 for the unlawful processing of a large number of citizens' health information. The COVID-19 test provider used WhatsApp groups at all its test centres, granting all of its employees unrestricted access to confidential information about citizens.
The Spanish DPA fined a bank €50,000 for sending commercial communications on the envelope of a letter to a client that had exercised their right to object.

A customer who had a dispute with an Amazon seller complained that the seller, Malagatrom, S.L.U., had published her name, address, mobile number, and her husband's name and mobile number in a public seller-feedback comment, after threatening to do so in a reply. The inspection found the complaint true and also found three other comments in which the company disclosed customers' personal data. The AEPD held that publishing the data on a public website had no lawful basis under Article 6 GDPR, and that the related confidentiality breach was absorbed into that single infringement. It fined the company EUR 4,000 and ordered it to remove the comments and prevent similar conduct within one month.

A physician denied to give any information about a child to his father and identified the mother as the only person entitled to receive such information. It was only after the HPDA intervention that the physician accepted to give access to the requested data by depositing to her lawyer, located at Chalkida city, a sealed envelope with copies of the medical exams. HDPA accepted that the physician violated also art. 12 par. 1 GDPR obligation to facilitate the exercise of applicant’s right of access by imposing as the unique way of access the obligation to travel from Athens to Chalkida city (80 Km distance) during the covid19 lock down when traveling was forbidden.The fact that the applicant couldn’t reach Chalkida city due to the covid19 restrictions should not be interpreted as a resignation from his right of access as argued by the physician.

The Spanish DPA fined Telefonica €75,000 (reduced to €45,000) for processing personal data without a legal basis. Telefonica had continued to call a data subject for direct marketing purposes after they had exercised their right to object.

The Danish DPA held that the general recording of phone calls by the Danish Business Authority without prior consent was a breach of the GDPR. It found that consent is the only legal basis for such recordings, which were used for the purpose of documenting the intimidation of employees and internal training.

The UK DPA fined a transgender charity approximately €29,250 (£25,000) for infringing Article 5(1)(f), 32(1) and 32(2) GDPR. Internal emails containing special categories data sent by the charity, which supports gender non-conforming children and their families, were publicly available online for over a year.
The DPA fined Jamk University of Applied Sciences €25,000 for unnecessarily processing the location data of its employees. The DPA also imposed a ban on the processing of location data.

The Spanish DPA fined an individual €1500 for sharing personal data related to the sex life of the complainant on a website. The DPA rejected the individual's claim that a BDSM submission contract is a valid form of consent, and a legitimate basis for the publishing of such personal data.

The AEPD fined an individual EUR 1,000 for using a third party's personal data to apply for a micro-loan through an online lending portal, without any legal basis under Article 6(1) GDPR. The complaint came from a court that had convicted the individual of minor fraud linked to that loan application. The individual did not respond to the opening agreement, so the proceeding went straight to a decision. The AEPD treated the conduct as intentional, which it counted as an aggravating factor.

A private individual shared on Twitter a video showing a man assaulting a woman while her young son tried to intervene. The faces of the woman and the child were not pixelated. The AEPD opened its own investigation and a sanction procedure for processing personal data (images) without a legal basis under Article 6(1) GDPR, proposing a EUR 10,000 fine. The respondent paid EUR 6,000 within the deadline, using both 20% reductions (acknowledging responsibility and voluntary payment). The AEPD therefore declared the procedure terminated under Article 85 LPACAP.

The Polish DPA fined a foundation approximately €3,000 (PLN 13,644) for failing to inform both the DPA and data subjects of a data breach. The DPA also ordered the foundation to communicate the personal data breach to the data subjects.

The Spanish DPA warned a Spanish city council for infringing Article 30 GDPR by not maintaining a record of its processing activities, and Article 31 of the Spanish Data Protection Act by not making a record of its processing activities available by electronic means.

The Luxembourg data protection authority opened an own-initiative investigation into a group of companies, focusing on video surveillance, and visited the premises of Société A (a bakery and pastry manufacturer) in March 2019. It found that a camera covered part of the public road and that ten cameras permanently filmed employees at their workstations, breaching data minimisation. It also found that employees and third parties (customers, suppliers, visitors) were not given the information required by Article 13 GDPR. The restricted formation fined the company EUR 12,500 for both breaches (the head of investigation had proposed EUR 17,000) and ordered it to bring its information to employees and third parties into line with Article 13 within two months. It declined to issue the proposed corrective measure on data minimisation because of the compliance steps already taken.
The ICO fined a claims management service approximately €235,000 for making more than 11 million unsolicited direct marketing calls over a six month period.

The Finnish DPA found that a controller (X) and a processor (Y) had failed to enter into a data processing agreement pursuant to Article 28(3) GDPR. It decided not to impose a fine firstly because the data processing operations had already ended, and secondly due to the very low turnover of Y and the fact that it had already filed for bankruptcy.

Seventeen people complained about unsolicited marketing calls made for the gas supplier ZENITH by its call-centre processor, One Way Private Company. The calls reached subscribers listed in the Article 11 opt-out register because an employee failed to apply the exclusion step to some cold-call lists. This happened from 28/11/2020 to 3/2/2021, and over 1.5 million calls were made in that period. The Authority fined the processor EUR 30,000 for breaching Article 32(2) and (4) GDPR together with Article 28(3)(c). It reprimanded the controller ZENITH for breaching Article 28(3)(c).

The Norwegian Privacy Appeals Board rejected a complaint where a data subject asked the DPA to require Microsoft to uncover the identity (via IP addresses used at login) of alleged hackers of their Hotmail account.
The Spanish DPA (AEPD) fined a controller €10,000 for issuing an invoice containing incorrect data in violation of the accuracy principle.
The Italian DPA (Garante) fined the Mayor of Messina €50,000 for publishing images of minors and disadvantaged individuals on social media in violation of Article 5(1)(a) and (b) GDPR.

The UK DPA found that an email data and marketing service violated the lawfulness, fairness, and transparency principle, since its email address database had no clear lawful basis and individuals were not informed that the service had acquired their personal data. Among other things, the DPA ordered the service to notify individuals whose data it processes of the information under Article 14 GDPR.

The Norwegian Privacy Appeals Board (Personvernnemnda) reduced an initial administrative fine from approximately €38,300 (NOK 400,000) to €23,950 (NOK 250,000) due to the DPA's long case processing time.
The Lithuanian DPA fined a sports club approximately €20,000 for processing the biometric data of its customers and employees in violation of Articles 9(1), 13(1) and (2), 30, and 35(1) GDPR.

IMY investigated Stockholm's public transport operator SL after media reported it would equip ticket inspectors with body-worn cameras recording image and sound. IMY found that SL's pre-recording technique (continuous recording stored for at least one minute) lacked a legal basis and breached data minimisation, that recording to establish the identity of passengers given a surcharge was unlawful and excessive, and that SL gave passengers insufficient information. Actual recording during ongoing threats was found lawful. IMY imposed a total administrative fine of SEK 16 million, split SEK 4 million, 8 million and 4 million for the three infringements.
The Polish DPA fined an insurance company approximately €35,387 EUR (PLN 160,000) for failing to notify a personal data breach to the DPA, as well communicate it to the relevant data subjects.

A person who was not a Magyar Telekom customer kept receiving unsolicited newsletters because a customer had mistakenly given the person's Gmail address. Repeated erasure requests were answered with unsubscribe links that led to a login page, which the complainant could not use. The Authority rejected the request to order erasure as moot, since the address had been deleted during the procedure. It found ex officio breaches of Articles 5(1)(d), 6(1), 12 and 17, plus a general practice infringing Articles 12(2) and 25(2). It ordered Telekom to change its practice so that exercising data subject rights does not require unnecessary extra conditions, and fined it HUF 10,000,000.
The Spanish DPA (AEPD) fined an energy company €12,000 for making marketing calls to a data subject that had signed up to a Robinson List.

The Danish DPA (Datatilsynet) reported the Vejle Municipality (Vejle Kommune) to the police for the failure to implement appropriate security measures and proposed a fine of approximately €26,900 (DKK 200,000).

The Information Commissioner’s Office fined a home improvement company approximately €153,000 (£130,000) for making more than 900,000 direct marketing calls from numbers that masked the company's identity, and that were in part directed at individuals who had opted-out.

The Belgian DPA issued a reprimand against a public authority that shared an audit report including personal data to third parties without a proper legal basis. In addition, the controller was found in violation of the GDPR for not answering the access request in due time.

A buyer paid a deposit on a flat to a real estate company in Zaragoza and received no data protection information. The company's reply to the AEPD cited the repealed Organic Law 15/1999 and did not meet the Article 13 GDPR information duties. The AEPD opened a penalty procedure proposing a EUR 2,000 fine. The company paid EUR 1,200 on 9 June 2021, using both 20% reductions for voluntary payment and acknowledging responsibility. The AEPD therefore declared the procedure terminated under Article 85 of the LPACAP.

The CNIL fined a DIY company a total of €500,000 for violating Articles 5(1)(e), 13, 17, and 32 GDPR and for infringing national provisions concerning cookies and unsolicited commercial communications.

The UK DPA (ICO) imposed a fine of €11,600 on Global One 2015. This charity infringed Articles 22 and 23 PECR by sending unsolicited marketing messages without consent and without providing a point of contact for individuals to refuse such marketing.
The UK DPA (ICO) imposed a fine of €11,600 on Papa John's (GB) Limited for sending unsolicited direct marketing messages to 168,022 individuals in breach of Article 22 PECR.

The CNPD opened an investigation into a company's video surveillance and vehicle geolocation systems and visited its premises in March 2019. It found that cameras permanently watched the reception workstation and the staff entrance and smoking area, that the information given to employees and third parties was incomplete, and that the geolocation software lacked individual access accounts and a proper retention limit. The restricted formation found breaches of Articles 5(1)(c), 5(1)(e), 13 and 32(1) GDPR and imposed a single fine of EUR 7,200. It also ordered the company to bring its Article 13 information into compliance within two months. No corrective measure was ordered on the geolocation system because that processing had been stopped.

The CNPD opened an investigation into a car dealership group's video surveillance and geolocation and, after an on-site visit in December 2018, focused on Société A. It found that two of its thirty cameras filmed the public road and six cameras permanently monitored employees at their workstations, breaching data minimisation. It also found that employees and third parties (customers, suppliers, visitors) were not properly informed under Article 13. The restricted formation fined the company EUR 7,600 and ordered it to bring its information notices into compliance within two months.

The CNPD ran a thematic audit campaign on the role of data protection officers and opened an audit of a transport company in September 2018. The investigator found that the DPO was not systematically involved in data protection matters, that his autonomy was not guaranteed, and that his monitoring and advisory tasks were not formally carried out. The restricted committee upheld the breaches of Articles 38(1), 38(3), 39(1)(a) and 39(1)(b) GDPR and imposed a fine of EUR 15,000. It also ordered the company to comply with each of these articles within four months.

The Italian DPA inspected Foodinho s.r.l. (Glovo group delivery platform) in July 2019 on its own initiative, looking at how it processes data of its riders through the platform and algorithms. It found unlawful processing breaching the general principles (lawfulness, fairness, minimisation, storage limitation), information duties, safeguards for automated decision-making and profiling, privacy by design and default, records of processing, security, DPIA, DPO notification, and the employment-law rules on remote monitoring. It ordered the company to bring its processing into line within 60 days (with algorithm and feedback checks to start within 60 days and finish within 90 more). It also imposed a fine of EUR 2,600,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

A patient complained that a dentist made him fill in a medical questionnaire asking about infectious diseases including HIV, and then declined to treat him after he disclosed being HIV-positive. The Garante found that the HIV information was collected without a concrete treatment purpose, since care was in fact refused, so the legal basis for processing health data fell away. It found a breach of the Article 5 principles and fined the dentist EUR 20,000, with publication of the decision on the Garante's website.

Following an inspection campaign on whistleblowing applications, the Garante examined the Bologna airport operator's use of the 'WB Confidential' platform supplied by a processor. The platform ran over unencrypted http, stored data unencrypted, and navigation logs on the whistleblowing site were kept without safeguards. The Garante found breaches of Articles 5(1)(f), 25, 32 and 35 GDPR. It fined the company EUR 40,000 for the breaches of Articles 5(1)(f), 25 and 32, imposed no fine for the missing DPIA given the early application period, ordered no corrective measures because the conduct had ceased, and ordered publication.

During a round of inspections of whistleblowing software, the Garante checked the 'WB Confidential' application that aiComply supplies as a processor to Bologna airport operator AdB. It found that aiComply used two other companies for system and application maintenance without any contract or authorisation as sub-processors. It also found the application ran over plain http, kept data in the database unencrypted, and had a System Administrator account shared by two people. The Garante held that this breached Articles 28 and 32 GDPR and fined aiComply EUR 20,000. It ordered the company to bring its processing into compliance and report back within 30 days, and it ordered publication of the decision.
The Romanian DPA fined a controller approximately €2000 (RON 9.852,2) for failing to cooperate with the DPA during an investigation by not providing it with information it had requested.

IMY investigated, after a complaint, the round-the-clock real-time camera surveillance of the vehicle halls at eight fire stations run by the Östra Skaraborg Rescue Service. The cameras also covered the spot where staff change into their emergency gear, so employees were filmed in underwear. IMY accepted that the public-task legal basis (Art. 6(1)(e)) existed, but found breaches of the fairness principle (Art. 5(1)(a)), data minimisation (Art. 5(1)(c)) and security/organisational measures (Art. 32(1) and 32(4)), since no instructions existed on how the footage could be used. It imposed an administrative fine of SEK 350,000, of which SEK 300,000 relates to Art. 5 and SEK 50,000 to Art. 32. The surveillance ended on 6 May 2021.

The Romanian DPA (ANSPDCP) fined a controller approximately €2000 (RON 9839) for failing to provide the DPA with requested information during an investigation. Furthermore, the controller received a warning for not fulfilling a data deletion request.

The Italian DPA temporarily restricted data processing by “PagoPA S.p.A” on its public services app, "app IO." It found that Google and Mixpanel Inc. were collecting and processing the data of identifiable users without obtaining their consent and without a legal basis. PagoPA S.p.A has thirty days to redesign the app to conform with the principles of Article 5(1) GDPR and to allow users to consent or object to the processing of their data.

The Norwegian DPA fined a company approximately €14,700 (NOK 150,000) for taking over an employee's work email account during her notice period without warning her, without giving her the opportunity to delete personal content, and despite her objection, thereby violating Articles 6(1)(f), 13, 17(1)(e), and 21 GDPR.

After a newspaper reported that millions of recorded calls to the 1177 healthcare advice line were openly accessible online, IMY opened supervision of the Region Sörmland board. IMY found that the board collected callers' phone numbers and municipality IDs to route calls to the provider MedHelp AB without giving the information required by Article 13, which also breached the transparency principle in Article 5(1)(a). The processing itself was found lawful and data-minimised. Because the lack of information affected a large number of care seekers, IMY imposed an administrative fine of SEK 250,000.

After a newspaper reported that millions of recorded calls to the 1177 healthcare advice line were openly exposed online, IMY opened supervision of the regional boards using the service, including Region Värmland. IMY found that callers were not informed that their phone number and municipality ID were collected so calls could be routed to the care provider MedHelp AB. Missing were the controller's identity and contact details, purpose, legal basis, access right and the DPO contact. IMY found breaches of Articles 5(1)(a) and 13 and imposed an administrative fine of SEK 250,000. The data minimisation and legal basis for the processing were found to be fine.

After a newspaper reported that millions of recorded calls to the 1177 healthcare advice line were openly accessible online, IMY opened supervision of the Stockholm health board. It found that the board, as controller, did not inform callers about its collection of their phone number and municipality ID, or about its later collection of call information from the provider MedHelp AB for follow-up and quality purposes. This breached Articles 13 and 14 and the transparency principle in Article 5(1)(a). IMY imposed an administrative fine of SEK 500,000 and ordered the board to provide the information within two months of the decision becoming final. The underlying processing itself was found lawful.

MedHelp AB, the care provider answering calls to the Swedish healthcare advice line 1177, was investigated after a newspaper reported that millions of recorded calls were openly accessible on the internet. IMY found four infringements: disclosing patient data to a Thai company, MediCall, without legal basis; leaving the call recordings on a storage server exposed without protection; not informing callers about the data processing; and not backing up the recordings. IMY imposed a total administrative fine of SEK 12,000,000 and ordered MedHelp to inform callers and to introduce proper backups within two months of the decision becoming final.

A Computer Sweden article in February 2019 revealed that recorded calls to the 1177 healthcare advice line were openly accessible on the internet. IMY found that Voice Integrate Nordic AB was a processor for MedHelp and stored the recordings on its Voice NAS server. The server was exposed to the internet without any protection, because of a misconfiguration, for an unknown period until 18 February 2019. IMY estimated 650,000 to 900,000 calls were affected, containing sensitive health data covered by professional secrecy. IMY held that Voice breached Article 32(1) and imposed an administrative fine of SEK 650,000.
The Spanish DPA ordered a processor (Amazon Web Services) to answer an erasure request from a data subject that had not been completed by the controller (a news website).

The Litigation Chamber of the Belgian DPA ordered the Belgian Special Tax Inspectorate to comply with a complainant's requests to exercise their rights under Articles 14, 15, 16, and 18 GDPR. The Chamber held that subjective information can constitute personal data under the GDPR, and that restrictions to data subject rights in a Belgian income tax law are formulated too broadly and are therefore not applicable.

Moss municipality merged its health-clinic IT system with that of Rygge municipality and converted about 28,000 patient records. The conversion produced many errors: vaccines wrongly registered, wrong pregnancy and substance-use data, and patient data exposed to staff without a need for access with no traceability. The Datatilsynet found that the municipality had done no risk assessment and insufficient testing, and that the conduct was negligent. It imposed an administrative fine of NOK 500,000, reduced from the amount first notified after the municipality's response and comparison with similar cases.

The UK DPA fined Solarwave Limited approximately €116,000 (£100,000) for sending direct marketing communications to individuals registered with the Telephone Preference Service who had not given their prior consent. In calculating this fine, the DPA considered, among other things, that Solawave Limited acted contrary to detailed guidelines it ought to have been aware of, and continued to make unsolicited calls pending the outcome of the ICO's investigation.

The Spanish DPA determined that the Spanish Tax Authority had complied with GDPR requirements when introducing a new biometric system used to register employees' working hours and building access. It further determined that the Authority had given data subjects adequate information about the system.
The Estonian DPA issued an opinion stating that a processor must respond to a pending access request or else face a EUR 2000 fine.

The Spanish DPA fined a company €26,000 (reduced to €19,600) for recording images of their employees' resting room and for not offering up-to-date information about the use of video surveillance at the workplace.

Two former employees complained that their employer, a small company, monitored staff through a video surveillance system inside its offices without informing them. The company said the internal cameras had been switched off since 2008 and that only common-area and perimeter cameras were active, and it answered the Authority's requests only after repeated reminders. The Authority found infringements of the principles of lawfulness/fairness/transparency and purpose limitation and of accountability. It ordered the company to remove the five internal cameras within one month and destroy any material collected, and fined it EUR 15,000.

The Italian DPA imposed a provisional limitation on the processing performed by the Mitiga Italia App, an app used to certify compliance with covid regulations by people wanting to attend sporting events. The limitation is be enforced for as long as necessary for the DPA to establish the legal basis of processing, and to establish whether the data processed was adequately limited.

The UK DPA fined the Conservative Party £10,000 in relation to 1,190,281 direct marketing emails sent as a part of its Brexit campaign. In particular, the DPA held that the Conservative Party had not collected valid consent for the 51 emails sent to the complainants in violation of the PECR, which implements the e-Privacy Directive in the UK.

The UK DPA fined a funeral plan service approximately €168,000 (£145,000) for sending direct marketing calls to individuals registered with the Telephone Preference Service who had not given their prior consent to receive calls. In particular, the various data providers that the service contracted with had failed to collect valid consent from individuals, who were not given a genuine choice about whether to accept marketing from third parties.

The Italian DPA ordered Associazione Rousseau, the owner of a digital platform for participatory democracy, to give “Movimento 5 Stelle,” a populist political group, access to the personal data of all its members. The DPA clarified that under Article 28(3)(g) GDPR, a processor must return all data to a controller that no longer wants to use its services.

In 2018 the Luxembourg CNPD opened a thematic audit campaign on the data protection officer (DPO) function and audited Company A. The investigator found that the DPO was not sufficiently involved in data protection issues, lacked necessary resources, and did not effectively fulfil the information and advice task. The restricted committee found breaches of Articles 38(1), 38(2) and 39(1)(a) GDPR, imposed a fine of EUR 18,000 and ordered compliance measures within four months on Articles 38(1) and 39(1)(a).

Between 2016 and 2018 UWV suffered nine similar data breaches when staff sent group messages to jobseekers via the 'Mijn Werkmap' environment and attached the wrong Excel file containing sensitive personal data. The AP opened an own-initiative investigation and found that UWV had not guaranteed a security level appropriate to the risk, a continuing violation of Article 13 of the old Wbp (until 24 May 2018) and Article 32(1) and (2) GDPR (from 25 May 2018 to December 2018). UWV had not adequately assessed risks, had not put in place the necessary technical measures, and had not checked or evaluated the measures it adopted. The AP imposed an administrative fine of EUR 450,000, raising the base amount of EUR 245,400 because of the seriousness of the violation.

The bank launched a customer portal, 'Min Side', in September 2019. A session verification fault let some customers see other customers' loan and contact details for about ten minutes. The bank notified the breach itself. The Datatilsynet found that the bank had no documented risk assessment and had tested the portal inadequately. It held that Articles 24(1) and 32(1)-(2) were breached and imposed a fine of NOK 400,000. The bank accepted the fine in advance.

The Czech DPA ordered a new first-tier decision of a case because in its earlier decision it did not properly carry out the balancing test in Article 6(1)(f) GDPR. It also held that the new decision should consider the application of Article 10 GDPR.

The Romanian DPA fined Vodafone Romania approximately €1,000 (RON 5,000) for not taking the necessary measures to prevent a data breach that lead to the transmission of certain customers' invoices to third parties.

A local health authority notified a personal data breach: a hospital admission notice for a medically induced termination of pregnancy was sent to a patient's general practitioner through the regional SOLE network, although she had expressly asked for it to be masked. A software bug at the external supplier caused it, and 48 similar cases were found between April 2018 and August 2019. The Garante found the processing unlawful for breaching Articles 5(1)(f) and 9 GDPR and Article 75 of the Code. It imposed a fine of EUR 120,000 and ordered publication of the decision, with no corrective measures because the conduct had ended and could not recur.

The health authority of the Province of Trento notified a data breach: because of a software error in its report publication routine, 293 health documents of 175 patients were made available to their general practitioners even though the patients had requested that they be hidden. 163 of the documents concerned data subject to greater anonymity protection, notably voluntary termination of pregnancy. The Garante found the disclosure lacked a legal basis and breached the principles of lawfulness, integrity and confidentiality and Article 9. It imposed a fine of EUR 150,000 and ordered publication of the decision, without further corrective measures since the conduct had ceased and the problem was fixed.

After a complaint filed with the AEPD against Vodafone España, the AEPD sent information requests that Vodafone did not answer. The AEPD opened sanction proceedings for obstructing its investigative powers (Article 58(1) GDPR), proposing a EUR 5,000 fine. Vodafone paid EUR 3,000 on 17 May 2021, using both 20% reductions (acknowledging responsibility and paying voluntarily). The Director therefore declared the proceedings terminated under Article 85 LPACAP.
The UK DPA fined a car finance company approximately €198,000 (£170,000) for sending unsolicited direct marketing messages without obtaining valid consent.

The Slovenian DPA held that a bar owner does not have a legitimate interest in monitoring the various rooms and outdoor terrace of the bar with video surveillance, but does have a have a legitimate interest in monitoring the bar counter and bar entrance. Accordingly, the DPA gave the bar fifteen days to adjust the viewing angles of its surveillance cameras to record only the counter and entrance.

Datatilsynet fined the City of Oslo NOK 400,000 for publishing a personnel case document on the eInnsyn public records portal. The document was a court summons containing sensitive data, including health information and details about the person's private life. It was sent on paper without a cover letter and was not marked as exempt from public access, so it was registered and approved for publication. It was publicly available for 5 hours before removal. The affected person alerted the municipality, which then removed the document.

The Belgian DPA withdrew a previous decision, considering that it was appealed by the defendant on the ground that he was not sufficiently informed of the grievance against him. The Litigation Chamber of the DPA reopened the case and gave the parties the chance to submit their arguments.
The Romanian DPA fined a controller €500 (RON 2,463.30) for violating its obligation to cooperate with the DPA during an investigation by failing to provide the information requested.

The Romanian DPA fined bank approximately €2,000 for the processing a complainant's personal data with out a valid legal basis, in enforcement proceedings for debts resulting from a credit agreement which he had no knowledge of.
The Spanish DPA fined Vodafone €50,000 for making more than 250 unsolicited commercial calls to a data subject after they had exercised their right to object.

The Norwegian DPA (Datatilsynet) upheld its decision to fine Innovation Norway NOK 1,000,000 (~€98,000) for subjecting the complainant to multiple credit ratings without a legal basis under Article 6(1)(f) GDPR.

An employee complained that DOPAKA, a municipal body, published on the Diavgeia transparency portal a board decision about his work conduct, identifiable through his initials, job, hiring date and workplace, and ignored his request to withdraw it. The Authority rejected the claim that the document was anonymised and found that DOPAKA had not cited any specific law requiring the posting, so Article 6(1)(c) was not shown to apply. Legitimate interests (Art. 6(1)(f)) cannot be used by public authorities performing their tasks. DOPAKA also failed to reply to or satisfy the erasure request. The Authority fined it EUR 7,000 and EUR 3,000 and ordered withdrawal of the act from Diavgeia.
The UK ICO fined American Express ('AMEX') £90,000 for sending 4,098,841 direct marketing communications to customers who had opted out from receiving these.

A local health authority told the Garante that the laboratory company Synlab Med had emailed it the positive Covid-19 serological test results of 31 patients who were not assisted by that authority, by mistake. The data included names, tax codes and, mostly, phone numbers and email addresses. The Garante found the processing unlawful for breaching the principles of Article 5 and Article 9 GDPR and imposed a fine of EUR 20,000, with publication of the decision. No corrective measures were ordered because the conduct had ended and the company had planned audits and training.

The Romanian DPA warned Telekom Romania for processing personal data for marketing purposes without a legal basis, and fined it approximately €2,000 (RON 9,851.40) for continuing to contact a data subject after they had exercised their right to object.

The Italian DPA received several complaints and reports about unsolicited marketing calls made for Iren Mercato using contact lists bought from third parties. The data had passed from website operators to Nethex and then to Iren Mercato without the data subjects' specific consent to transfers between independent controllers. The Garante rejected the company's legitimate interest argument and found breaches of Articles 5, 6 and 7 GDPR. It fined Iren Mercato EUR 2,856,169, banned further promotional processing using third-party lists lacking valid consent, issued a warning about incomplete evidence given in the investigation, and ordered publication of the decision.

An employee of the Municipality of Bolzano complained about the monitoring of internet traffic and individual web access of municipal staff, which was used to open a disciplinary procedure, and about a medical-check request form shown to the department director. The Garante found that the municipality collected browsing logs of about 1,000 employees without a valid legal basis, adequate information or a DPIA, and that the extraordinary medical check procedure also breached the Regulation. It declared the data unusable, fined the municipality EUR 84,000, and ordered it to anonymise workstation data in the web logs and delete the logs already recorded. It also ordered it to report on the measures it would take.

The Spanish DPA warned a regional Department for Public Education and Universities for not adequately informing their workers about a biometric identification system that was in the process of being implemented.

A former student of a different vocational institute (IEK) complained that IEK ALFA, run by the controller, sent him a promotional email without his consent and ignored his access and erasure request. The controller said he had left his email himself, that one employee sent the message by mistake, and that his data was deleted after his objection. The Authority found breaches of the principles of purpose limitation, lawfulness and transparency, and of the rights of access and erasure (no reply to the data subject, no valid opt-out address). It imposed a fine of EUR 5,000.

The Greek DPA fined a service provider €5000 for failure to properly execute a data's subject request for erasure due to a technical error which meant that their personal data had been duplicated on the company's servers. The DPA found that 79 other data subjects had also been affected by this error.
The Luxembourg DPA fined a controller €1900 for using their videocameras to record images of public spaces and buildings, and for applying an excessive retention period to such images.

The Luxembourg DPA (CNDP) fined a controller €1000 for capturing images of a public space using their video-camera system, and for not providing necessary information about the video-camera system in accordance with Article 13 GDPR.

The Portuguese DPA ordered an educational institution to stop using a proctoring app to evaluate students online, as the app infringed the principles of lawfulness, purpose limitation, and data minimisation. The DPA also ordered the institution to instruct the relevant processor to delete all previously stored data.

The Hamburg DPA (HmbBfDI) issued an order under the GDPR's urgency procedure prohibiting Facebook Ireland Ltd. from processing personal data from WhatsApp for its own purposes. The order is immediately enforceable.
The UK's DPA fined a company offering digital contact tracing services £8,000 for sending marketing emails to subscribers without obtaining their free and informed consent.
The Slovenian DPA (IP) held that an eGovernment portal had violated Article 32 of the GDPR by failing to ensure that documents posted on its bulletin adequately secured personal data.
The Romanian DPA fined a controller approximately €2000 (RON 9 851) for breaching Article 32 GDPR by publishing the resignation request of a former employee on its employee WhatsApp group.

A policyholder complained that his health data and other data obtained through a hospitalisation insurance were used for other purposes and passed to third parties listed in the insurer's privacy statement, without a choice. The Litigation Chamber had fined the insurer EUR 50,000 in decision 24/2020, but the Market Court annulled it because the insurer had not been able to defend itself fully. In this reconsideration the Chamber again found breaches of the lawfulness and transparency principles, the accountability duty and the information duties (Arts 5, 6, 12, 13), including lack of a demonstrated legitimate interest for staff training and CCTV storage. It reduced the fine to EUR 30,000, as the Article 6 breach covers only two purposes and the insurer had already revised its privacy statement.

The Norwegian DPA (Datatilsynet) fined the Norwegian Olympic and Paralympic Committee and Confederation of Sports (NIF) about €123,656 (NOK 1,250,000) for a data breach in which the personal data of 3.2 million people was exposed online.

The Norwegian DPA published a draft decision notifying Disqus that it will be fined approximately €2.5 million (NOK 25 000 000) for unlawfully processing personal data for programmatic advertising purposes. In addition, the DPA found that Disqus breached transparency and information requirements by not providing data subjects with adequate information about the company's tracking, profiling and disclosure of personal data.
The Icelandic DPA stated that a municipality and a trade union did not comply with Article 6(1) GDPR when sharing complainant’s data without a legal basis.

The Icelandic DPA held that a police officer had not violated the law on the processing of personal data for law enforcement purposes, by refusing an access request to personal data registered in the Schengen Information System (SIS).

The Spanish DPA fined an energy company €1,500,000 for not providing sufficient information to data subjects under Article 13 GDPR, and for not implementing adequate measures to avoid or mitigate risks related to the data processing under Article 25 GDPR.

The Spanish DPA fined an energy company €1,500,000 for not providing sufficient information to data subjects under Article 13 GDPR, and for not implementing adequate measures to avoid or mitigate risks related to the data processing under Article 25 GDPR.

The Icelandic DPA fined a controller responsible for an electronic school management system €23,585 for not implementing appropriate technical and organizational measures which resulted in a data breach affecting 424 children.

The Austrian data protection authority found that neither the GDPR nor the Austrian law implementing the GDPR will apply to the transfer of health data between two individuals via WhatsApp, as such processing fall's under the GDPR's household exemption.

The EDPS found that the CJEU had breached data protection requirements in relation to web tracking. They were found to have insufficient information on their site, and a banner which did not allow users to reject cookies.

Following their decision to fine Google €100,000,000 for not complying with the cookies regulation, the CNIL accepted Google's adjustments and decided to close the case. However, the DPA stated that this only refers to the precautionary measures taken in their original decision, and reserved the right to further analyze Google compliance with the cookies regulation and the latest CNIL guidelines on the matter.

A complaint was filed against a bank for passing a customer's data to a company without consent. The data protection authority sent the company three requests for explanations, but the company never collected any of the letters, so they were deemed delivered. The authority opened a separate procedure and found that the company breached the duty to cooperate and to give the authority access to necessary information. It imposed a fine of PLN 22,739 (equivalent to EUR 5,000), taking the failure to give access to information as the most serious breach.

The Hungarian DPA (NAIH) held that the recording of an employee's telephone conversation was undertaken without a valid legal basis and without providing information on data processing to the complainant. When a company wishes to record employee telephone conversations, it must assess whether other measures having less impact on personal data can be taken.
The Icelandic DPA held that a credit rating company was permitted to use information on previous entries in the default register when preparing the credit ratings.

The Belgian DPA fined a financial institution €100,000 for failing to implement adequate security measures to control employee access to the Belgian Central Credit Register in violation of Articles 32, 25, 24, and 5(2) GDPR.

The Spanish DPA fined Equifax, a credit ranking agency, €1,000,000 for failing to comply with Article 5(1)(a), 5(1)(b), 5(1)(c), 5(1)(d) and with Article 14 GDPR. The authority ordered Equifax to stop the processing and to delete the related database.

The Italian DPA found that the disclosure of certain databases regarding COVID-19 by schools in the Province of Modena may enable the identification of pupils and their health status, even where data which directly identifies the pupils is removed.

The Belgian DPA reprimanded an entity in charge of paying family allowances to its members for failure to comply with Articles 4, 5, 6 and 24 GDPR, in relation to the processing of a data subject's 'household composition' data.

The Belgian DPA held that in this specific case, concerning a father and mother sharing parental authority, the request to have data about the child erased, introduced by the father alone, had not been submitted in a way that could be accepted. The Belgian DPA also found several other violations of the GDPR by the controller.

The Polish DPA fined a satellite platform operator €250,000 for violating Article 24(1),Article 32(1), and Article 32(2) GDPR for not implementing appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure the security of personal data when cooperating with a courier company. See comment.

The Italian DPA found that a Government decree implementing a system to regulate citizens’ movements and access to events during the Covid-19 pandemic violates Articles 5, 6(3)(b), 9, 13, 14, 25 and 32 GDPR.

Data of activists and sympathisers of a political party leaked from Google docs. It did not inform the DPA on measures taken, including data subject notification. The DPA levied a fine, ordered notification of data subjects and security measures.
The Luxembourg DPA issued a warning to a controller that had not adequately informed its employees about a geolocation system used in its company vehicles.

A data subject complained in February 2020 about the online booking form for follow-up visits at the Tor Vergata hospital foundation, which collected health-related data over unencrypted http and without the Article 13 information. The Garante found breaches of the integrity and confidentiality and transparency principles and of Articles 13, 25 and 32. No corrective measures were ordered because the hospital had meanwhile switched to https and provided the information. It imposed a fine of EUR 15,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

The Spanish DPA found that an impact study carried out by the Spanish Government on daily commuting trends during the COVID-19 pandemic was carried out in compliance with the GDPR, since the Government had implemented appropriate measures to prevent data misuse.

The Romanian DPA fined a processor approximately €1500 (RON 7,331.85) for failing to implement appropriate measures to prevent data loss, and for not processing data according to the instructions of the controller.

A neighbour complained that cameras installed at a bar with a terrace were aimed at public space without authorisation. The AEPD found that the cameras captured an excessive part of the public pavement, neighbouring buildings and parked cars without justification, and that the posted sign did not identify the controller. The operative part finds an infringement of Article 5(1)(c) GDPR and imposes a fine of EUR 1,500 on the individual operating the bar, described as the lowest band for this type of infringement.

The Romanian DPA investigated a food company after a complaint that it filmed employees with cameras in offices, changing rooms and the canteen. It found excessive video monitoring of employees in changing rooms and the dining area, justified by protecting goods and deterring theft, which could be achieved with less intrusive means. Consent in an employer-employee relationship was not freely given and no other legal basis was found. The company was fined RON 24,362.50 (equivalent to EUR 5,000) and ordered to bring video monitoring into line with data minimisation and to reorient camera angles.
The Spanish DPA (AEPD) fined a landlord €3000 for violating Articles 5(1)(c) and 13 GDPR in relation to a video surveillance system in an apartment building.

A hospital doctor used a patient's health data, including identifiable clinical history, diagnostic images and 22 surgical photographs, in slides for a medical congress and a 'best clinical case 2017' prize. The slides were later published on the website of a surgical society. The patient had not consented, the doctor did not seek authorisation from the health authority (the controller), and the data were not effectively anonymised. The Garante found breaches of Articles 5(1)(a) and (c), 6 and 9 GDPR and fined the doctor EUR 5,000, with publication of the decision. No corrective measures were imposed because the slides had been removed and disciplinary proceedings had been brought against the doctor.

The Garante received a complaint that a person's data in a food-aid application filed with the City of Palermo had been accessed by an unauthorised operator of a third-sector association. The City ran a 'Centrale Unica Aiuti Alimentari' platform and gave third-sector helper organisations a single shared login per organisation, which let operators search applications by tax code (even the first three characters) and see personal and income data. The Garante found breaches of integrity and confidentiality, data protection by design and default, and security of processing. It fined the City EUR 40,000, taking into account the large number of data subjects, the roughly two-month duration and health data, against the emergency context and the City's later security measures. No further corrective measures were ordered, and the decision is to be published.

A complainant said INPS never answered two certified-email requests to its Bolzano office asking how his contribution statement had allegedly reached third parties. INPS admitted the lack of reply, blaming an email mishap, and argued the events were too old and the records no longer kept. The Garante found that INPS failed to answer the access requests within the legal time limits, breaching Articles 5(1)(a), 12 and 15 GDPR. It fined INPS EUR 12,000 and ordered publication of the decision. It took no action on the original access to the contribution statement because of the time elapsed.

The Polish DPA held that printouts from a bank's IT system could not constitute evidence of proper communication to a data subject regarding its intention to process his personal data for the purposes of a creditworthiness assessment. In the absence of other evidence, the DPA concluded that the bank had breached its information provision obligation.

The Spanish DPA decided that a controller could not require a data subject to identify themselves with their national ID, when this document had not been asked for in the first place. In this instance, the controller had no reason to doubt the identity of the data subject.
The Norwegian DPA fined a controller €3,500 (NOK 35,000) for sharing a CCTV recording of a data subject vandalising its property with the data subject's employer, without a legal basis.

The Dutch DPA investigated TikTok Inc. on its own initiative and found that between 25 May 2018 and 28 July 2020 it gave its privacy policy to Dutch users, including children, only in English. This breached the duty in Article 12(1) GDPR to inform in clear and plain language, especially children. The AP rejected TikTok's arguments that the Irish authority was competent (the infringement ended before 29 July 2020) and that the rule was too vague (lex certa). It started from a base fine of EUR 525,000 and raised it to the category maximum of EUR 750,000 because of the gravity and duration, imposing a fine of EUR 750,000.

The Belgian DPA held that, for lack of a legal basis pursuant to Article 6 GDPR, a notary cannot consult the national register for natural persons in order to obtain personal data for other purposes than those defined by the law and within the scope of their profession.

The Luxembourg DPA fined a controller €2800 for processing geolocation data from their fleet of company vehicles without an adequate retention period and without providing all the necessary information to their employees.
The Slovenian DPA held that on the basis of Article 15 GDPR it is not possible for an employee to obtain information about the data processing activities of other employees within a hospital.

The Slovenian DPA held that a building manager can disclose data to a unit owner without the consent of others, if the disclosure is necessary for the proper determination of contractual obligations. This information may only be provided in a manner that precludes disclosure by unauthorised persons.
The Icelandic DPA held that a primary school was not permitted to disclose information about a child to a consulting company after termination of collaboration.
The Slovenian DPA held that self-employed individuals do not enjoy protection of their personal data when operating as business entities.
The AEPD fined a controller €3000 for abandoning documentation containing personal data next to a building, which was considered a data breach and therefore a violation of Article 32(1) GDPR.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) fined a controller €3000 for the infringement of Article 32(1) GDPR, due to a data breach that was caused by the abandonment of several envelopes containing confidential medical data in a field.
The Spanish DPA fined Vodafone €150,000 (reduced to €90,000) for processing personal data without consent or any other legal basis.
The Swedish DPA reprimanded a Swedish bank for not responding to an access request for 5 months following complaints filed with DPAs in Germany and Austria.

The Romanian DPA published a press release saying that it had finished an investigation of Telekom Romania Mobile Communications in February 2021. It found that the company had not applied adequate technical and organisational security measures. Data of 99,210 customers, including national ID numbers, were disclosed or accessed without authorisation because wrong billing addresses went into a database passed to a debt-assignment partner. Separately, 413 customers' MyAccount data was accessed without authorisation. The company was fined the equivalent of EUR 10,000 under the GDPR, and RON 15,000 under Law 506/2004. It was also ordered to review its security measures and set up regular testing.

The Slovenian DPA stated that video surveillance performed by an individual from his private facility or from his private property to the neighbor falls under the exception of "personal use". Therefore, the DPA has no jurisdiction under the GDPR.

The Italian Garante investigated Fastweb after hundreds of complaints and reports about unwanted telemarketing calls made by Fastweb and its sales network. It found seven groups of violations: no control over the chain of data collection by sales partners, use of third-party contact lists without valid consent, defects in the 'Call me back' service, inadequate security against repeated unauthorised database access, failure to notify the resulting data breach, inaccurate data when handling data subject rights, and marketing without valid consent or a valid legitimate-interest basis. It imposed a fine of EUR 4,501,868, equal to 5% of the maximum fine (EUR 90,037,367), together with corrective orders, two processing bans and publication of the decision.

Two complainants received repeated promotional emails from OneDirect despite objecting by certified email, and their requests and the Garante's information requests went unanswered because the company's PEC mailbox was not monitored. The company could not document consent, did not produce its own record of processing activities, and cooperated poorly with the authority. The Garante found breaches of Articles 6(1)(a), 7(1), 12, 24, 30 and 31 GDPR and of the Italian Code. It banned further promotional use of data without documented consent, issued warnings, ordered organisational measures to answer data subject requests, and fined the company EUR 30,000 with publication of the decision.

A man complained that the publisher of the newspaper La Stampa had not answered his request to erase or anonymise his data in an old online archive article about a court case, and had ignored his request of 14 March 2019. The Garante found the erasure request unfounded because the archive use is compatible with the original journalistic purpose and the article had been de-indexed from search engines. It also took no action on the request to update the article, since the complainant had provided no documents on later developments. It upheld the complaint on the failure to reply to the data subject's request, rejected the 'involuntary oversight' excuse, and fined the company EUR 20,000, with publication of the decision.
